title: Eddie Condon as a musician and chord man
summary: Though his four-string guitar was inaudible out front, Condon supplied the right chords and little background breaks that Davison could hear.

story.theme_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section: instruments and players
story.community_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section's changing role

blocks.x: Now, let's lay it out - just as flat
out as you can, what Eddie Condon's musical contribution was---

Well, a lot of people say they never could hear him play; I can understand that. That he never had an amplified guitar and it was a four-string and a four-string guitar isn't very loud and that's why they say - what hell, doesn't he play up there; what's happening? You never hear him. But, we covered him up. But, Ed was a great musician.

Oh, marvelous. God, when we rehearsed sometimes, he was the guy who came up with the chords-- he'd say - here is the chord; he'd get it for you. And, you know, when you've beenwith Ed on bus rides, train rides---
When you say rehearse, you're not talking about Condon's you're talking about other places too; you used to play a lot of other shows outside of Condon's.

Yes - well, there were T.V. shows and our Town Hall things; we'd get things straightened out. But, Ed was always there with the right chord and he knew what the hell he was doing;and a lot of people, you know - Ed wouldn't play a solo. You --- could you in the band hear him?
Oh, sure. He was right on top of me.
And, you used to hear him play-ing--
Well, up front it would be impossible, you know.
I think Eddie Condon spent his career playing for you.
No, but on bus rides or on train rides, when I was with Ed, he'd get his guitar out; you should hear some of the gorgeous chords he played.
